subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have spoken on this Bill before but we on this side still have to rise to continue putting the case that we have been putting. It seems, however, that the Government is unable or unwilling to listen. There was some suggestion last week from a Conservative to my left, whose riding escapes me for the moment, that we were not taking this matter entirely seriously. Let me put that to rest first of all. We take this issue very seriously indeed. I do, particularly, coming as I do from the Province of Newfoundland.
The basic argument against this Bill is that it hits those people in Canada who can least afford the added burden, namely, the low income people. You can make all the arguments you like about the family allowance Bill per se, but if you add it to the other measures that have been taken that impact on low income people in various parts of Canada, it is true that they are going to be hit very hard.
The family allowance will be deindexed from 1986 onward. The child tax credit, although it will be raised to $454 per child in 1986 and thereafter, will be deindexed from 1989 onward. The child tax exemption will be reduced from $710 per child in 1986.
We talked about the tax exemption last week, Mr. Speaker. The $50 federal tax deduction is being eliminated and some families will pay $100 more in federal tax. The federal sales tax is being increased. If you add it all together, there will be a net reduction for low income people. This coming year and thereafter low income people across the country will get less money net than before as a result of Bill C-70 and the other measures taken by the Government. That is an unacceptable situation, Mr. Speaker, because of the economic situation existing in Newfoundland and in provinces like Nova Scotia, particularly in the Cape Breton area. It seems that the Government has written off the Atlantic region completely.
Let me put that in context. The Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), who is the Chairman of the Finance Committee, suggests that all of these measures have to be taken because the deficit has to be reduced and the fiscal house has to be put in order. He says that to take up the slack, we must put the private sector front and centre. That makes sense in theory, but not in reality.
In Newfoundland and in the Atlantic area the private sector is weaker than it is in other parts of the country. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) tells us continuously about the 300,000 or 400,000 jobs that his Government has created since coming to power, but that may or may not be true. That may or may not stand up in analysis. But the very studies to which the Prime Minister is referring that confirm, to him at least, that the Government has created 300,000 or 400,000 confirm also that only 8 per cent of those new jobs have occurred in the Atlantic area. The private sector in that area is weaker than in other parts of the country.
Our economy has depended upon Government intervention and government support systems of economic survival until now. The case I want to make is that we must not take away those programs, we must not cut those programs, and we must not tamper with the social security system, until such time as we have put something else in its place.

speechtext: What do you mean by "until such time"? Not at all.

If the Government does that, there will be a double whammy in the Atlantic area. Not only are the new jobs not being created, but we are losing support in terms of Government programs, transfer payments and social security programs on which we have depended until now.
That is one of the main reasons my province came into Confederation. We are a new province in Confederation. 1 was not born in Canada. 1 was 13 years old, as I keep saying, when my people came to this country. That is true; 1 was 13 years old in 1949. One of the reasons we joined Canada was the kind of economic and social security which Canada could offer us. That is one of the reasons we are part of Confederation. Only 52 per cent of our people voted to join. The very issue on which Newfoundlanders voted to join Canada is being tampered with now and is being taken away as far as we can see. This is happening at a time when we have the highest cost of living and the highest unemployment rate anywhere in the country.
Statistics Canada will show that our unemployment rate is something like 20 per cent. I think it is more than that. If we add in the hidden unemployed, those people who have given up

looking, the unemployment rate is something like 40 per cent.
I would say that among young people it is more like 50 per cent. That is the situation which has to be addressed and put in context in this debate.
At the same time that we have that high unemployment rate and that high cost of living, what else is happening? People are being laid off in the Department of Fisheries. Hundreds of people will be laid off in that Department this year. Everyone knows how much we depend on the fisheries. Everyone knows how many public servants there are in our province in that Department. Transport is being cut. The latest cut about which we are hearing and we want confirmed, and I hope disavowed, is that there will be a complete and utter shut-down of Terra Transport, which is CN Rail in Newfoundland. It is the last remaining vestige of railway service in Newfoundland and it will be done away with by the Government. We have to add all these factors together.
It is not enough to say that we have signed the Atlantic Accord and that it will be the salvation of our people. It will not be, because those jobs will not come for years. When they do come, how much will we make out of the Atlantic Accord? Perhaps it will be $200 million per year, but the provincial deficit is something like $300 million per year. It will not be the salvation of our people.
I have put these points on the record to show that it is not only this Bill on family allowances. This Bill, along with other measures, will have a very serious impact on people in my province and on people in the Atlantic area. The Government has to recognize that. If it looks at nothing else, it should look at the polls and see the reaction of people to this particular issue. That kind of attitude must change. They cannot tamper with those programs. The Hon. Member to my left who said that they cannot be tampered with in any way is quite right. However, the point I am working is that at a time like this it is particularly unacceptable and unbrearable for people to be subjected to the kinds of cuts we are experiencing, not simply in Government programs upon which we have depended for a long time. The small craft harbours budget is something else which we use to create jobs. Even make-work programs have changed now so that people in rural areas are disadvantaged. Projects such as Canada Works are more difficult for people in rural areas to take advantage of because they involve training elements and that kind of thing. There seems to be a general, over-all thrust or drift to the right, which is having a completely unbearable impact in my particular area. This family allowance Bill is something which highlights it.
People have rights to fair and equal treatment. We cannot have blanket policies which fit everywhere in Canada. We know that. Joey Smallwood used to tell the story from time to time about Procrustes' bed. Procrustes was a Greek who operated what we would call a motel today. He had one bed, and every traveller who came to that inn had to fit that bed. If he was too long, he chopped him off; if he was too short, he extended him so that he would fit the bed. That cannot be done in Canada. Canada is a country of regions, and we must have a sensitivity to that reality. One of the things that is
absent, as I see it, in the present Government is a regional development policy. I have asked for it in the House before; I have asked for it to be enunciated. It has not been enunciated. What happened to DREE? What has been put in its place? Where is the regional development policy of the country? Not all areas of Canada are equal. If they come in with blanket programs saying that they will slash willy-nilly across the country, it will impact more heavily on those people who are already in an unequal position. That is the reality and that is the situation.
I return to my main point. The Government has not announced what its economic development policy will be for Newfoundland. I hope the Hon. Member for Mississauga South will address this issue because he is a proponent of free enterprise carrying the load. The thesis is: "You are going to be all right because we are going to put private enterprise front and centre and it will be the saviour of the country". I am saying that there is no evidence that that is happening in Newfoundland. There is evidence in the meantime that the public service programs and social security programs on which historically we have heavily depended all the while that we have been in Confederation are now being chopped and nothing is being put in their place. Not only is that wrong in principle, as my friend to my left said, but it is particularly wrong at this stage in our development because it will simply sink us economically altogether.
I want to see the reaction of the Premier of Newfoundland not only to those measures but to the measures which will impact upon us very soon-today, tomorrow or in the next few days-with the cut-backs in CN Rail and the complete wiping out of Terra Transport in Newfoundland. The only reaction can be to fight it with all our might. I hope there will be a consolidation or a firm coalition of all those who are interested in fighting that battle. It is a battle which has to be fought. This a bad Bill in and of itself. It will impact negatively on low-income people. If we add the family allowance changes, the child tax credit changes, the child tax exemption changes, the sales tax and the deindexation of the income tax, there is a net reduction to low-income people. Those people cannot bear that in principle and should not have to bear it in principle. They should not have to bear it at a time when their economic future is in grave doubt and grave uncertainty. That is the reality, that is what is happening. I do not know how often we have to point that out to the Government. It seems that any such plea is falling on deaf ears, come from where it may. The latest group to add its voice to those of others is the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops which has been very active in my province as well. Indeed the Pope, when he was in this country and spoke in Flat Rock, Newfoundland, addressed this very issue. Surely he is more eloquent than I am, but I have a responsibility today to stand in the House of Commons and echo what he said and what the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops said. They said: "We have noted the rationale for the restructuring of social programs, namely, deficit reduction". Whatever the merits of such a strategy, society must not succumb to an ideology of restraint that
January 20,1986

subordinates human dignity and human needs to abstract economic theories. That is the point. You cannot succumb to an ideology of restraint that subordinates human dignity and human needs to abstract economic theory.
Low-income people, no matter where they live, have a right to be served by the Government of Canada and the Parliament of Canada, and have a right to those services that they have historically enjoyed: They say: "It is our fear that the social and human impact of the proposed changes to the family allowance will only add to the already widespread suffering of our families, particularly families headed by women".
According to the recent report on poverty by the National Council on Welfare, the number of families living below the poverty line has increased for the fourth year in a row. The most vulnerable groups include one-parent families headed by women, unattached young people and the elderly. That is the constituency that this Party has historically tried to defend by bringing in those social security systems and regional development policies and by making sure that people who did not have were helped in some way. There has to be that Government intervention in areas of this kind. I am speaking particularly on behalf of my own province.
This Bill is wrong in principle because it hits, along with other measures, particularly at low-income people who should not have and cannot afford to bear that burden. It is particularly wrong at this particular time when the economic situation is so fragile and in such great difficulty, and in the absence of any regional development policies to show the regions of the country that are have-not regions that you have some way of securing their economic future. That is the reality of this Bill. That is why we should defeat it if we can, and that is why we have to do whatever we can, use every vehicle or mechanism at our disposal, to point out to the Government the error of its ways and to hope, in the final analysis, in the eleventh hour, that it will change its mind.

I appreciate the question, Mr. Speaker, and the Member that it is coming from. The issue in 1949 obviously was not indexation, because indexation occurred later. We did not really have inflation in 1949, but we encountered inflation thereafter. As a result of that inflation it was decided to index family allowances, and indeed other measures, so that low-income people could keep up with costs that they were confronted with. There was no indexation obviously at the time of Confederation.
The point that I was making was that we negotiated the terms of union, a contract with Canada in 1949. One of the strong selling points made by Mr. St. Laurent and his Government at that time, and by the Parliament of Canada, was that Newfoundland would be eligible for social security payments such as family allowances. If you had to take in Newfoundland one symbol of the support for and the importance of Confed-

There were other things that we encountered too, such as funds for economic development, and later on programs for economic development. At the time of Confederation in 1949 when that contract was made between the two sovereign countries, one of the outstanding issues that sold Confederation, only to 52 per cent, but it did sell, was the issue of family allowances. I am saying now that our people are looking at this issue and thinking back about how important this and other Government programs have been to them. They will be judging in a historical context the doing away with what was very important to them and one of the fundamental and essential points on which they agreed to come into this country.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps the House will forgive me a slight digression at the outset of my speech. I would like to respond very briefly to the exchange we just heard between a Conservative Member and a former Liberal Minister who is now on this side of the House.
Coming from the Conservative side of the House, we heard what is now the classic rationale for Conservative policy. This rationale began not very many days ago when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was asked both in and out of the House why he shut down a refinery in Montreal. He indicated
January 20, 1986

that he was simply trying to catch up with the Liberal Party which had shut down three refineries while he had shut down one. If it was all right for the Liberals to do it, the Prime Minister said, then that was a coherent, cogent reason for a Conservative Government to do the same thing.
We are now hearing the same thing about family allowances. A Member from the Conservative side of the House asked a former Minister if he would admit that the Liberal Party cut back on family allowance indexing when it was in power. To understate it considerably, that does not persuade me that it is right for the Conservative Party to do today what was wrong for the Liberal Party to do a decade ago.
On the other hand, we heard the former Minister of the Crown make a backhanded compliment to members of my Party by saying that one day we may govern, and we certainly believe that that is true. If I understood him correctly, he added that in the meantime, we have to deal with issues. The implication was that the Liberals deal with issues between elections but when they get elected they forget them.

Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, you will excuse a somewhat partial person if he says that that sort of sums up this little debate and my views of these two old Parties.
I do wish to turn to the substance of the issue and not simply deal with some of the arguments that have been made, although it seems to me that those arguments are pretty germane to what is going on right now. In my judgment, today is really a sad day for Canada, Canada's families, Canada's children, Canada's parents and particularly Canada's mothers.
As far as my Party is concerned, the central issue involved in the debate is the question of fairness. Later on today, the Conservative majority will rise unanimously to demonstrate by its vote its concern, not for fairness but for unfairness. That will dramatically illustrate that the Government is not only insensitive to the claims of fairness but is also insensitive in the face of opposition to this particular measure on the part of a wide range of groups that represent every part of our country.
Many very good points have been made about family allowances in this debate. However, for me there are two crucial aspects to the history of family allowance in Canada. First, when family allowances came into being, our society recognized by state action the value of children by earmarking a very specific sum of money to be directed to children in society. That was an important action. Normally, in most of our transactions, a good part of which is totally justified in a market economy, people have the freedom to choose how they dispose of their incomes. That is part of what freedom is all about. However, my Party has long held the view that the allocation of financial resources in society ought never to be exclusively determined by market considerations.
Historically, the fundamental reason we came into being was that we favoured the view that society itself, through its elected men and women, ought to interfere with the marketplace constructively, positively and without embarrassment to
Family Allowances Act, 1973
decide that there are certain collective goals for the community as a whole that ought to be met by spending income. When we decided many years ago on family allowances, we were saying as a society that children and families are important and that the state is earmarking a particular sum of money to go to the children of our society. That is important and has become part of our social history.
The second important aspect of family allowances is something which, though not intended as such, was immediately perceived and has remained, and that is, what it has meant for many women in Canadian society. The point that has now been recognized by members of all Parties but is not made today is that the only cheques many women in Canadian society receive in their own names are the family allowance cheques, and that is a very important consideration. I am sure Members on all sides of the House have run into women in rural Canada, urban Canada, the Atlantic provinces, the West, downtown Toronto and downtown Montreal who have said that the family allowance cheques, though perhaps they are not an awful lot in dollar value except for low-income families, are important to them because the cheques come in their names. These two points are very important. I would suggest that a Government sensitive to these elements of social justice in our past would not be changing them now for the future.
Some 40 years ago family allowances were introduced. I would argue that they have an important place in the shared set of social values which most Canadians support. Without going into all the details of the history from that point in time onward, I do wish to mention a few crucial points.
We heard from a former Liberal Minister who gave what I would call a selective view of the history of family allowances. He failed to mention that in 1971, after they had been introduced, members of the Liberal Party, with a majority Government, attempted to abolish family allowances entirely. They did not attempt simply to reduce them or curtail their increments but, in 1971, the Liberal Party tried to abolish them entirely. They did not get away with it. They backed down after a prolonged debate in the House of Commons.
Then, in the early 1970s-and I say so with some pride and without trying to be sanctimonious-in the early days of minority Government, which held office from 1972 to 1974, a whole range of social programs were indexed. At that time I was proud to be chairman of my caucus. 1 took part in the discussions. We made the case that social programs, most of which but by no means all-which is important in terms of their effects-must go out to people who need the money. We made the case that when the economy is inflating, those social programs should be indexed to reflect the change in the cost of living. I wish to say to our Liberal colleagues in the House that they did not automatically respond by saying "Isn't that a good idea. Let's do it". There was something to do with power and its maintenance involved. We put it to them bluntly that if they wanted to remain in office one of the things they had

I say to the Minister responsible for this Bill, and I know he has had this referred to him a number of times, that when he was on this side of the House and when he spoke on the subject on September 6, 1973, he joined in support of the indexation principle. Following that debate the Minister moved to the other side of the House and he has shifted his argument. However, I want to be as fair as I possibly can to the Minister. He responded to one of my colleagues earlier in this debate in defending his current position. He admitted that when he was on this side of the House he took the position that full indexation was to be supported. Now that he is on the other side of the House, he says that we need a change because of the deficit. That is what he said in the House recently. He said that the deficit has increased significantly as a proportion of our GNP.
I wish to say to the Minister two things in this respect. First, in a document which he prepared as a forerunner for a discussion of pensions he said that there would not be any change in terms of cutting back on social programs, in this case pensions. He said that money from those programs would not be allocated away from them to deal with the deficit. This year, when the economy was inflated and when the debt was just about as real, he made a commitment that there would be no change in social programs in order to use that money for the deficit. However, he is now doing just that.
Second, I want to say to the Minister that it is our view that if you are taking revenue to deal with any economic problem faced by a Government-a Government which will take money from pensioners or recipients of family allowances-it should never do so except in the final result. By God, it should certainly never do it when it is giving a $500,000 capital gains tax gift to the rich in Canada.

subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: I say to the Minister that the argument simply does not wash. As Leader of a social democratic Party I would be prepared to say that at certain times absolutely everyone must pay his or her share. In wartime, or under certain other circumstances, I can understand that, and in this category I include pensioners and recipients of the family allowance. However, I say this should be done only if there is a real crisis. I am certainly not saying that we have that type of situation in Canada today. 1 do not accept that, when we continue to have one of the most unfair tax systems in the world and this Government keeps that unfair tax system in place.

I also want to say that although indexation was brought in by a minority Government, after the Liberals regained a majority they began the process of cutting back on

That is right. I have also looked after Manitoba, which is more than the Minister of National Health and Welfare is doing. We certainly looked after our provinces. That is one reason the Tories will lose in Manitoba. The people of that province know who cares about them.
The fact of the matter is that this is a family allowance reduction. It can only be counted in those terms. It is drawing money away from families. I take with some amusement the last speaker saying that Canadians would be out in the streets clapping with wild applause when they get a 31-cent increase in their family allowance cheques this month. Will that send them rushing out to buy services? The problem with attacking family allowances-and in some way it is an easier target-is that the benefits are oftentimes invisible or hidden. Many of the families who receive family allowance often cannot get their problems or issues out of the forefront.
I have conducted an examination of families in my riding and have found out that the family allowance is absolutely essential for many mothers to buy services for their children which are otherwise not available to them. It may provide some better medical help or some decent counselling. It may simply provide bus money or transportation money to allow them to visit or go somewhere else, something which allows them to round out their lives.
One cannot simply apply calculus and say that it is of more benefit to one family than to another. There is an entitlement involved. If we return to the Marsh report of 1943, we see that it contained a basic principle which we are trying to defend, that is, that the opportunity to have a family-and it is a rare opportunity-also carries certain costs which cannot be pigeon-holed in the Department of National Health and Welfare or in the Department of Finance. Those are costs which every family has in terms of its own unique arrangements and needs, so we put some small amount of discretionary income into their hands so they can apply it where they feel the most pressure. Sometimes it may concern schooling or purchasing a certain consultative service in the health field. Nevertheless, it gives each family a certain entitlement or trust provided by the collective society to help them make their choices. If we erode that entitlement and do not replace it with anything else, we reduce their level of choice and their ability and capacity to help their families and children seek out the support services they need. This is why the debate in the House is such an
important one. It should encompass the full range of options and choices.
I am sorry the Minister of National Health and Welfare has left momentarily. I was very saddened after the debate on deindexation affecting senior citizens. He was heard to utter a statement that the Government was withdrawing from the field of social policy innovation and reform, that it would no longer engage in it because it was burnt badly. Now it will simply draw into a fetal crouch, not use its mind and imagination to seek out the different alternatives. That is a serious mistake; it is a fundamental error. Instead, the Government is nickle and diming Canadians to death. It is picking away at the income base of low and modest income Canadians. That should not be the action of a federal Government which says that it cares, a federal Government which was elected on fond promises of giving families more hope and aspirations. Families cannot be given more hope and aspiration if $1,000 per year is to be taken out of their pockets by 1990. There is no way any Tory can justify doing that. That does not even take into account the hidden costs which are being brought in every day. We see the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) adding a few dollars to air transportation, licensing and certificates. We see other costs related to farmers. The total basket of costs is rising and income is going down. Yet, we heard the last speaker saying that they cared. It is very difficult to rationalize caring when we look at the facts.
Obviously we oppose this legislation, not only on the grounds of what it is doing in the context of family income but also because it represents the wrong direction or approach to dealing with the issues of family life. We must encourage the Government to open and broaden its approach and not to base its revenues upon some kind of restrictive, punitive equation put forward by the Minister of Finance. We should look at the revenues available and see how they can be applied in a more flexible, varied and sensitive way to families. Then we will have a healthier country and a healthier economy. The Government's proposition is a self-defeating one.

Mr. Speaker, I think all of us in this caucus feel that this is a pretty dark day for Canada's children as well as for the women of Canada and for families generally. The family allowance is a very important contract that we as a country have with Canadian families.
We have now come to the final day of debate on the third reading stage of Bill C-70, the Government for the second time having imposed closure on this debate. We are very disappointed that the Government at no time has really reconsidered this Bill based upon the very massive protests of many Canadian groups regarding the deindexation of family allowances.
There have been consultations, advice, appeals and protests made by well over 100 organizations, all of which I could list if I had the time. These organizations appeared last spring when we debated the reform of the family benefits and when the Government invited them to get involved in consultation. Many of them gave expert opinions at that time, opinions which were disregarded. Despite feelings that this consultation had been a farce, these organizations returned to the legislative committee which dealt with Bill C-70 to give their opinions.
I am referring to groups from every walk of life. Women representatives of poor people's groups told us from firsthand experience what it means to be trying to budget for a family with lower welfare rates and how important the family allowance, and a fully indexed family allowance, is to them because when they go to the grocery stores, they have to pay the full price of the food and other items they need for their families.
We heard from community groups from all provinces. We heard from many women's groups. I would say that there has been a massive stimulation of the women's movement across Canada as a result of this Bill. We heard from women's groups from practically every province of Canada and particularly from the Province of Quebec where over 50 or 60 organizations formed a new coalition to protest this Bill and present their views on it to committee. Of course, these are views that very dramatically and militantly oppose Bill C-70.

January 20, 1986

We heard from many churches. We heard from the United Church, from the Canadian Council of Bishops and from the Anglican Church, all of which oppose Bill C-70. We heard from many different labour groups. We heard from child care groups across Canada. We in our Party heard from native groups. We did not hear from them in committee because the committee did not agree to hear from native women's associations. However, we received letters and have spoken with them directly and we know that many native women's groups object to this Bill.
We heard from parent-teachers' associations right across Canada, associations which represent a huge network of parents with school-age children. They oppose this Bill very strongly. We heard from social work experts and from social policy groups including the CCSD, the National Council on Welfare, NAPO and many other associations including the Canadian Council on Children and Youth, a very strong opponent of the Bill.
The Government has paid no attention to these representations. It spoke of consultation, yet these groups were unanimous in their opposition to this Bill. The organizations presented fact after fact to support the very negative, retrogressive, cumulative effects of this Bill as well as the effect it will have by symbolizing what the Government is doing to Canadian families.
For months now, petitions have been flowing in from ordinary Canadians right across Canada. It has been very difficult for mothers with young children to involve themselves physically in this protest by going to meetings and organizing in the way the old age pensioners did last spring. However, there is no question that this has been the largest mass petition campaign that we have ever seen in the House of Commons. As an example of that, my office just sent over the petitions that came this weekend. I suppose there are another 500 separate petitions here which came in only two or three days. The petitions are flooding in from all parts of Canada. Yet the Government has been ignoring them.
1 know the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) received all kinds of petitions directly but he has not mentioned this to the House. There have been telegrams and letters sent to the Government. The people have tried everything they can think of to try to get the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) and the Prime Minister to change their position on this matter.
This is the Government that talked about consultation and about listening to people. I know from talking to people that the people are very disillusioned at this point. Over 100,000 people have signed petitions opposing Bill C-70. That is the largest petition campaign ever launched, and the petitions are continuing to flow in. I would say that the Government ignores these petitions at its peril.
There is no question that there has been a wave of disillusionment and lack of confidence in this Government. There is the feeling that most of the promises the Government made have now been ignored.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, if you will agree, I will call it one o'clock and resume later.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF CHANGES ON CANADIAN ARMED FORCES PERSONNEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadian Armed Forces personnel and other groups of Public Service employees are furious at the Government because of changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act. As of January 5 those people are no longer eligible to collect UIC benefits because of pension incomes and severance pay. That is unfair, Mr. Speaker, and I will tell you why.
Many Armed Forces employees are forced to retire as young as 40 years of age. That is a condition of their employment. Naturally, they want to embark upon a second career. While they look for that second job, they should be eligible for UIC benefits. The changes say that they cannot collect UIC benefits while they look for work. If other Canadians can collect while on a job hunt, why can't these people? Their pension incomes will not pay the bills, which is why they go back to work.
These people are not milking the systems; they are in between jobs after they retire. They deserve those benefits. After all, they paid into the UIC fund for years. However, when they need it, the Government takes it away.
My office has been flooded with calls from people who are worried about the effect of these changes. They are worried about grocery and utility bills. The Government must take off its blinkers, open its eyes, and look at how its policies are hurting Canadians. I call upon the Government to reverse this decision immediately.

S O. 22 FISHERIES SUCCESS OF SALMONID ENHANCEMENT PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Salmonid Enhancement Program in British Columbia has been an incredible success story. SEP, as it is known, was initiated in 1977. It was designed to increase the population of the Sockeye, Coho, Chinook, Chum and Pink salmon, and the Steelhead.
Results to date indicate SEP production has become an important part of the West Coast fishing industry. In 1984 alone, 20 per cent of the value of the salmon catch in commercial, sport and food fisheries was a direct result of enhancement facilities. For those who are into cost-benefit ratio factors, the SEP ratio was about 1.6 to one. As well, the Salmonid Enhancement Program contributes substantially to job creation in remote communities such as those on the west coast of Vancouver Island.
We are now in a transition phase. SEP I is over and SEP II will soon begin. It is important that our commitment to salmon enhancement be maintained and expanded. Acknowledging that it is no longer 1977, and that our public debt has grown substantially since then, we must ensure that we utilize whatever means are available to fund fully this worth-while program.
Those who benefit from salmon enhancement must join the Canadian Government in a partnership which ensures a growing commitment to grow fish. When the production of salmon is brought back to historical levels of abundance this nation will benefit for generations. In other words, salmon enhancement enhances the future of Canada.

CELEBRATION OF FIRST MARTIN LUTHER KING DAY IN UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today inaugurates a new national holiday in the United States which honours the life of Martin Luther King. It is a commemoration which many Canadians will want to share as Martin Luther King embodied a spirit which was universal in its meaning and impact. There is a tendency nowadays to look back at the 1960s as a time of disruption and disorder. In reality it was a time when men and women of all races and backgrounds sought to find a way to be free. They sought to break the tradition of years of discrimination and inequality. For some of us who lived, worked, and studied in the U.S. during the time of the civil rights movement, it was a profound experience to observe this human struggle which was so pure and divine in its attempt to achieve change for mankind.
All Canadians can honestly say that we share with the Americans their memory of the meaning of this man and the cause he represented so well. We commit ourselves to the ongoing struggle for equality which he represents. As Robert Kennedy said when he learned of the assassination of Martin Luther King, "Let us dedicate ourselves to what the Greeks wrote so many years ago: To tame the savageness of man and make gentle the life of this world".

Canadian firms which wish to export their products south of the border. We are not seeking to open the borders between the two countries as the Opposition would have Canadians believe. It makes sense to secure and enhance access to the rapidly growing U.S. market which in 1984 alone purchased 75 per cent of our exports and generated 2 million Canadian jobs.
To set straight a second Liberal misconception, our Government is actively seeking to expand world trading markets. The Japanese Prime Minister said during his visit that he is impressed by our growing interest in Pacific Rim Trade. Our Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) has just returned from meetings in the U.S., Australia, and New Zealand, and is about to embark on a two-week trade tour of Asian countries. We have also offered to host the next GATT meeting in Montreal. The national trade strategy document tabled at the First Ministers' Conference in Halifax stresses our Government's commitment to international trade. I hope I have set the Liberals straight on this very vital issue so that they will stop misleading Canadians.

speechtext:
Last December 20, the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) drew my attention to the fact that he wanted to obtain complete photocopies of certain petitions and that he had been advised that, according to our practice, he could not have a photocopy of the signatures but could indeed have a look at those petitions.
I checked the precedents and I must confirm to him that the practice of the House of Commons has been that petitions presented by Hon. Members may be consulted upon request, but there has been hesitation in the past about providing copies of the signatures on the petitions. There are many reasons for
this, but the fact remains that petitions presented in the House are public documents and that, in my opinion, any petitioner signing such a document knows full well that a third party may consult the document and obtain the name of petitioners. The petitioner may or may not give his or her address, for that does not change anything to the petition and is not contrary to our Standing Orders.
I must say to the House that I would be reluctant to order that petitions be photocopied at the request of the public at large, but the question to be determined is whether a Member has the right if not the privilege to obtain a copy of one or more petitions presented in the House. It seems quite logical to me that, if a Member may present a petition in the House, the same Member or another Member may also obtain a copy, including the signatures. If a petition comes to the House through an Hon. Member, it seems to me that a copy may be taken out by a Member and, as in many other cases, Hon. Members are responsible for what they do with it.
Therefore I have asked the Clerk of Petitions to send a complete copy of a petition to a Member who will ask for one.

3.	Were representatives of CFS pensioners consulted on the action taken to commit inflationary interest earnings on CFSA assets in respect of pensioners and other beneficiaries towards reducing past and future service employer pension costs in respect of current employees and, if not, for what reason?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board

1 and 2. Before 1975, the actuarial valuations of the CFSA were based on a 4 per cent interest assumption. Rates of future salary increases and inflation were not projected.
In the 1975 valuation, the rate of interest was assumed to be
6.5	per cent per annum. Salary increases were assumed to be
5.5	per cent annually. These rates included an implicit assumption of 3 per cent inflation.
If no implicit assumptions for inflation had been used, the other economic assumptions could be regarded as being 3.5 per cent for real interest rates and 2.5 per cent for real salary increases. The effect of using an implicit inflation assumption of 3 per cent and therefore interest and salary increase assumptions of 6.5 per cent and 5.5 per cent, respectively, instead of 3.5 per cent and 2.5 per cent was to:
(a) decrease the CFSA actuarial liabilities by $2,438 million. Of this amount approximately $2,090 million could be

attributed to using a discount rate of 6.5 per cent during the plan members' retirement years, instead of 3.5 per cent; and
(b) reduce the full employer annual current service cost that would have been required from 19 per cent to 10.8 per cent of contributory payroll. Of the 8.2 per cent of pay decrease, about 6.2 per cent of pay is attributable to using a discount rate of 6.5 per cent interest rather than 3.5 per cent during the retirement period of plan members.
3. Representatives of Canadian Forces pensioners were not consulted about the change in economic assumptions used to value the CFS Account. The benefits of pensioners were not affected by the change in these assumptions. The assumptions were changed to enable realistic cost comparisons with private sector plans.

subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO AMEND

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Epp (Provencher) that Bill C-70, an Act to amend the Family Allowances Act, 1973 be read the the third time and passed.

subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that 1 have 13 minutes left, not enough time to tell how strongly we oppose Bill C-70. We are joined by over 100 organizations that have appeared on Parliament Hill and by many more than 100,000 petitioners who oppose the deindexation of the family allowance so very strongly.
Why is the NDP and all these groups and citizens protesting so very strongly? It is for the same reason that we opposed the Liberal's six and five deindexing and the earlier cuts made by the Liberals to the family allowance. First of all, Bill C-70, as we have said many times, is an attack on families. The family allowance cheque is the only family benefit that goes to all families that are rearing children. It recognizes the costs and responsibilities that parents take on when they raise children. It is the way in which taxpayers, who do not have children, contribute to the rearing of the next generation. It recognizes the value of children and of parenting. It shows that we are a caring society. It is also a very important means of subsidizing the heavy costs of larger families, a point that the Federation of Labour from P.E.I. pointed out was not stressed enough in committee.
By refusing to index the family allowance to the full cost of living the Government is not only taking money from children in real terms but is denying all the principles of this very important universal social program that 1 just mentioned. It is really denying the fact that this program is a social right to Canadian parents. It is a social contract between their Government, their children, and themselves. It is this contract that is being eroded.
This gives very bad signals to parents. It tells them that kids will have to pay for the deficit, that parenting is not important to the Government, that the Government is willing to allow family allowance to be eroded over the years-and that is where the significant decrease comes-and that children and families are not a priority of the Government. Those are the signals that people are getting, and the Government should realize that. The Ministers and Members sitting in the House should realize that this is a very serious and very negative matter from a political point of view.
Bill C-70 is an attack on women. We heard from the National Action Committee on the Status of Women, from the Canadian Advisory Council, and from many, many women's groups across Canada. This has aroused the anger of women so much that in Quebec a very strong and very determined new coalition of 60 or more organizations was formed which will continue to protest to the Government. They have lost all confidence in the Government and its actions.
As my Leader said this morning, women are concerned because they need that cheque for their kids, they deserve it, it is their right, and it should be fully indexed. They are also concerned because, in most cases, the cheque comes to women in their own name. I do not think that many men, who have always been in the workforce, realize what it means to a woman who has been raising kids in the home, who has been working very hard and gets no financial recognition, benefits, or adequate pension as do people in the workforce. The one
January 20,1986

thing she does get is a family allowance cheque which is hers. 1 am sure that in most cases she uses it for the children, but it is she who gives it to her children.
In the case of low income women, as they told us, this is money that the mother uses to buy food, especially toward the end of the month when the welfare cheque has been used up. To Canadian women the Government's decision to deindex means a reduction in the value of the family allowance cheque, and they feel that this is insulting, degrading and humiliating. It makes women very angry. They will not forget that anger, I can assure Hon. Members in this House.
The family allowance is little enough as it is. If the Liberals had retained full indexation and done what they should have done as a social commitment and a human right, we would have had family allowance cheques over $50 a month today, and that is the least they should be.
It is incredible that the Government would try to fool women and play around with this important program. The Minister put out a press release before Christmas saying that cheques would not be reduced but increased in January. He even put the cheques out ahead of this debate with an increase of one cent per day per child. The amount should have been four times that to cover the real costs of living.
We have heard from many people that Bill C-70 will be hardest on small families. It will be hard on large families who have a fair income because the cost of raising several children is very great. This Bill will be particularly hard on single parent families, 90 per cent of whom are headed by women who are poor.
The Minister can mouth his platitudes saying that he wants to help those in greatest need. Members who spoke this morning repeated that message but the facts show that that is not true. The family benefit programs and the steps taken in the Budget will hurt poor families badly. I will give some facts to substantiate that statement.
We heard from many mothers on low income and many social policy groups that deindexation is hardest on the poor. I know women in my riding who after using up their welfare cheques use their family allowance cheques. By the end of the month they are out on the streets. I can tell Hon. Members that because of Bill C-49 these women are out on the streets getting picked up and are subject to criminal charges. How do you think women and mothers feel, Mr. Speaker, when they know their Government cares so little for them that it is cutting the cost of living increases?
Bill C-70 is regressive social policy. We heard this repeatedly from social policy groups. One woman parliamentarian-I was really disappointed to hear her-said it is progressive. That is ridiculous. Combined with other Budget measures, it favours the rich and hurts the poor.
The National Council on Welfare and the Canadian Council on Social Development have this documented. The National Council on Welfare said that over the next five years a single
Family Allowances Act, 1973
mother with two children earning $15,000 annually will lose nearly $2,000 under the Government's Budget. On the other hand, a one-earner couple at the $80,000 a year level will gain nearly $6,000. It is incredible, isn't it, Mr. Speaker? The child tax credit is also being deindexed after three years. We sometimes forget about the child tax exemption, which will be reduced by deindexing. Higher income people will get a reduction for capital gains exemptions and a much higher ceiling on non-taxable RRSPs. Although the poorest families will have an increase in the child tax credit-I hope Members are listening because they keep giving out myths-the increase in the child tax credit does not come until 1987. In the meantime, in 1986 sales taxes imposed on the poorest families will be much higher than the increase in the child tax credit.
How can the Conservatives argue that the Budget helps the poorest families? They are either uninformed or unintelligent-I do not think that is true-but they must be deluded and certainly very cynical if they continue to repeat that argument.
The savings from the reduction on the indexation on family allowances also takes money from the lower income families according to the Canadian Council on Social Development. Their research shows that as a result of 3 per cent deindexation the Government will retrieve $49 million in 1986 alone. Of these savings, $33 million will come from families whose incomes are under $50,000. Average and poor families are being hit by Bill C-70, the families raising children.
The cumulative effect of deindexing the family allowance is another thing we must remember. It is only a little bit of money, a quart of milk a month, starting this new year. On the other hand if we look at what happens over the years with deindexation, the Canadian Council analysis shows that if inflation continues at 3 per cent, in 20 years time the family allowance will be only with $18 a month instead of $32, a loss of $168 a year. The child tax credit-get this-will be reduced to $326 from $384 today even though during part of that period there is an increase in the child tax credit.
The other thing we do not realize is that the turning point for income eligibility for the child tax credit is also affected. The CLC says that in 20 years time only those earning $14,000 a year, extremely poor families, will be eligible for the child tax credit. People up to the $26,500 income range are eligible today. This plan is insidious. As the years go by the family allowance wil be eroded, proving that the Government is attacking a universal program.
Bill C-70 also contains a section giving the Minister power to declare missing children as presumed dead. Child finder groups and parents with missing children are very concerned about this section. We think it should have been withdrawn. Native women have a special plea but were refused being heard. The Bill has a tremendous impact on their families and communities.
Bill C-70 represents a final betrayal by the Government which will come back to haunt it. The Government promised consultation. That promise has been a complete farce. Very qualified groups who were heard at committee twice unani-

January 20, 1986

mously opposed deindexing. Their consultation has been ignored. They will not ignore the Government, I know. The Government promised to protect universal social programs. Remember universality was sacred. I have already shown how universality has been attacked by Bill C-70.
Remember the Leaders debate, Mr. Speaker. The Prime Minister said he was going to be very sensitive to women's concerns, that women would have equal participation in society and that he was going to focus on women. He is focusing on women, all right. He is attacking women and their children. Women have told us over and over again that they have lost confidence in him. Even the Government advisory group has said how strongly it opposes this Bill.
The Conservatives said and the Minister who is sitting in the House says repeatedly that they want to help those in greatest need. The facts show that Bill C-70 and the other Budget measures are hurting families in greatest need. That is more rhetoric and another promise down the drain. The Government said it would recommend cuts to social programs when the economy improved. The Government now says the economy has improved, that there are more jobs, yet the Government is not willing to reconsider its stand.
We urge the Government to put a sunset clause in Bill C-70. We tried for amendments in committee and here at report stage so we could look at the Bill in a year if the Government would not do away with the Bill. We were ignored which shows that the Government either lied to the people about its intentions or it is lying now when it says the economy has improved.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Gabrielle Bertrand (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words at the third reading stage of Bill C-70.
The Bill was debated at length during second reading. It was studied in great detail in committee, and whatever could be said against or in favour of the Bill has already been said. In fact, today is the twenty-ninth day of debate on this piece of legislation.
During the next three years, this Bill and the amendments to the Income Tax Act concerning child benefits will gradually replace the present system with a fairer and a more sensible substitute, while maintaining the basic principle that families with children are entitled to certain benefits that are not available to families without children.
The proposed set of reforms guarantees that the highest after-tax benefits will go to families with the lowest incomes and that payments will be reduced progressively as a family's income increases. That is not the case at the present time, when a family with an income of over $30,000 receives higher after-tax benefits than a family with an income of $10,000.
I get the impression that the Opposition, especially the Liberal Opposition, tends to forget that between 1974 and 1984, it supported measures that made a fifty per cent cut in social programs. In 1976, the same Opposition reduced family allowances from $25 to $20 per month, reduced and finally eliminated the fifty-dollar child tax deduction in effect at the time, reduced the exemption for children from 16 to 17 years old, and finally, in 1982, the same Opposition capped indexation of family allowances at six and five per cent.
In fact, considering only what happened in 1976, if family allowances had been fully indexed to the consumer price index without interruption from 1974 onward, monthly family allowance payments would have been $51.83 per child this year, instead of $31.00 as is now the case.
Now, to the Members of the other Opposition Party who are such staunch defenders of the underprivileged. Did you tell those people about whom you are so concerned-and I am sorry to see the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) leaving the House now-did you tell those people the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth? Did you explain to them that the purpose of this Bill is indeed to give more money to the poorest among them? Would the Hon. Member for Vancouver East tell me whether she is prepared to go back to her riding this weekend and explain to the head of a single-parent family who earns $10,000 that, thanks to our new legislation, within five years this parent will have $250 more to raise his or her family?
Will the Hon. Member for Vancouver East be able to tell the parent that, because he or she will have $250 more, she will vote against the Bill this evening?
How does one explain this situation?
We have realigned our social policies under other amendments, particularly with respect to the child tax credit. Will Members of the Opposition tell families earning $10,000 a year that their child tax credit will be $734 in 1985, $768 in 1986, $908 in 1987, $1,048 in 1989? Did you tell that to your constituents?
If we examine the measures announced by our Government to help families we find that, generally speaking, the child benefit system will be changed somewhat over the next few years, but always to the benefit of poorer Canadians.
I said earlier that our family policy is an employment policy as well. If the father, the mother or the children in that family find work within the coming weeks or months, it will certainly compensate for the missing 94 cents on their monthly allowance cheque. In my opinion, that is more important to a family. Quebec's economy has been steadily recovering. Ever since the election, we have created, in Quebec alone, 136,000 jobs, that is an average of 9,067 jobs per month, compared with a total of 37,000 jobs created by the Liberal administration in 55 months.
It is clear that requests will continue to be made for still more money to help the poor in our society, to improve their living conditions, something we can understand. We fully support this concern for social justice.
The situation of families with children changes constantly. The federal programs designed to help these families cannot always automatically adapt to changing conditions. Therefore, it is sometimes necessary to reorient these programs, and that is the purpose of Bill C-70. We believe that we have adopted a realistic and equitable approach and we intend to continue to work in this direction.
Last December 5, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) announced the creation of a parliamentary task force on child care in Canada, to deal with the future orientation of policies in view of the changing needs of Canadian families. In our development policy, we are offering women, as an example, a labour market promotion and integration program to help them acquire the professional qualifications they need to meet the requirements, for some jobs as well as a practical knowledge of the labour market. In the health caucus, we have been studying for the past few weeks all aspects of poverty. We are concerned about these families and children who are living in poverty in Canada. We have heard experts deal with the subject: Mr. Ken Battle, Executive Director of the National Council on Welfare, Mrs. Sylvia Gold, of the Council on the Status of Women, Senator Brenda Robertson, who is familiar with this issue since she is a former Minister of Health from New Brunswick, the former Minister of Development, and in the coming days, we shall be hearing Mr. Michael Walker of the Fraser Institute in Vancouver. This is what we have been doing to help those who need it the most. In addition, we shall develop other social policies as our economy improves in the future.
January 20, 1986

Bill C-70 is a controversial piece of legislation. The Opposition parties and a number of groups and individuals have denounced it. Their arguments have not convinced me, but I respect the sincerity and the beliefs of most of them.
Like I was saying earlier, as our economy improves, the Government and the Department of National Health and Welfare hope to do even more for those really need it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had hoped to address the last stage of this Bill in a very general way by outlining the concerns of the Liberal Party and myself as the Health and Welfare critic regarding Bill C-70 which will deindex family allowances. However, after hearing some of the very technical arguments placed before us today, I feel almost compelled, and I will do so, to refute some fo the technical arguments made about this Bill so that we may draw our own conclusions at the end of the debate.
It seems to me that there are two basic arguments that Conservative Members have been using this afternoon. The first is that the total package of child benefits including the family allowance, the child tax credit and the child tax exemption will compensate for the reduction in family allowance.
Family Allowances Act, 1973
That was inherent in the questions that were put to the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) by the Hon. Member from Edmonton and the Hon. Member from Calgary. I think a few moments will be required to carefully consider the technicalities involved here.
That argument does not take into account the timing of the increases and deductions that are part of this program. Let me therefore begin with that premise and hope that Hon. Members opposite will understand exactly what it is they will be doing to low-income families. Indeed, Conservative Members have created the perception that the proposed changes to the total package of child benefits will compensate for the reduction of income to families following the deindexation of the family allowances. The other perception that is being created is that the end result will be a fairer distribution of benefits; that is to say, a greater proportion of benefits will go to families with lowest incomes. Unfortunately, neither of these highly desirable outcomes will occur. The reason for that is that the practical, negative effects of the proposed changes are not being recognized.
The single major problem with examining the three programs from a fiscal perspective is that the timing of the increases in the deductions are not being placed in the context in which they are going to occur. As an example, the reduction in the family allowances is to begin in January 1986, as soon as this Bill has passed. As a matter of fact, as I indicated in the House in December in debate and during Question Period, the Government did not even wait until the Bill was passed by Parliament before it presumed to change the figures that were to be placed on the family allowance cheques.
The deindexation will begin in January 1986. I hear from Members opposite that the child tax credit is being increased by $70. What the Government does not make clear is the fact that the $70 increase in the child tax credit will not be received by families until April 1987, some 14 months from now, because the child tax credit will not fully impact on families until another year goes by as it is only given out at income tax time. Quite simply, a family will lose the benefit of indexation for 14 months while awaiting the reported compensating adjustment. The Hon. Member from Edmonton and the Hon. Member from Calgary indicated that this was supposed to compensate, but they are going to have to be forced to admit that it will take 14 months before anyone, regardless of family income, will receive one benefit from the child tax credit.
In addition, there will be a second reduction for some families because this Bill lowers the turning point or the point at which one receives partial reduction of the child tax credit from $26,330 per year to $23,500. We lost the argument regarding that point in committee. As a matter of fact, the committee recommended that the turning point be much higher than that which is indicated in this Bill. We recommended that the turning point should be Statistics Canada's definition of family middle income which is $34,000 to $35,000 per year. Through this Bill, the Conservative Government has indicated that it feels that a family that earns $23,000 per year is sufficiently well off and does not require

January 20, 1986
Family Allowances Act, 1973
the full benefit of a child tax credit. Hence, families are going to begin to lose benefits under the child tax credit at that income level.
I will now deal with the import of these changes and I hope Hon. Members will listen carefully. The result of these changes is that between January 1986 and April 1987, all families in the country, regardless of income, will have their family allowances reduced by approximately $30. This shortterm loss will be significant in and of itself but it will not begin to compare with the combined over-all effects of the proposed changes.
The Government will choose to proceed with its changes despite opposition from individual families. We have heard of the petition campaign that was launched by the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party. As well, I must admit that there have been some back-bench Conservative MPs who have had the courage to present petitions from their own constituents outlining opposition to the family allowance deindexation. Despite all of that, despite individual families showing displeasure at the Government's intentions and despite the professional service groups that are opposed to this Bill, a net gain will only occur to those families with incomes of less than $10,000 per year. The cumulative total gain after four years for those families will be $76. More important, all families with incomes of more than $10,000 will experience a net loss of income. That is because Conservative back-bench MPs are not taking into account when the family allowance will be deindexed and when the child tax credit will impact on families. I will not even deal with the child tax exemptions which, I believe, properly belong in Bill C-84.
Another argument has been running through the minds of Conservative Members in this debate. They claim that the result of the changes will be a fairer distribution of benefits or that a greater proportion of benefits will go to families with the lowest incomes. If that had been the intent of the Bill and if that had been the intent of the Government when this debate was launched some 15 to 16 months ago, the Government could have brought forward a Bill that would have had the agreement of all three political Parties. Instead, we ended up with the worst of both worlds.
I believe there has been a betrayal by the Government of the trust placed in it by the electorate on September 4, 1984. The people evidently trusted the Conservative Party during the election campaign of 1984 and the few months following the election. They believed the Government when it said that universality was a sacred trust not to be tampered with. They believed the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) when he indicated in the social policy review that any savings which would be found in these programs would be redirected to those families who need it the most as opposed to committing it to deficit reduction. In the Bill before us we see the full truth of the Conservative social policy. In effect, what we have is a social policy which is Robin Hood in reverse, and 1 have used that phrase before in this debate.
In a very technical way let me speak to Conservative Members of Parliament who have used that second point in their speeches, that is to say that there will be a fair distribution of benefits. Statistics Canada states that some 78 per cent of Canadians live in urban centres. In its annual review of poverty published in May of 1985-just 10 months ago-the National Council on Welfare indicated that a family of four living in a moderate to large urban centre with a family income of less than $19,000 a year would be living in poverty. 1 ask Hon. Members to bear that in mind because the argument here is that this Bill will aid those families who need it the most. The net effect of the proposed changes on families with incomes of less than $20,000 is that they will experience a loss of child benefits and, subsequently, a loss in their capacity to provide an adequate level of food, clothing and shelter for their children. Futher, it is generally accepted that the major beneficiary of the child benefit programs are well-to-do families. The effect of deindexation will have the most negative effect on lower income families. As a result of this Bill's passage, and I have no doubt that it will be passed, in excess of $16 million will be withheld from families living below the poverty line. I think that is a shocking indictment of a Conservative Government's social policy. What is more shocking is the temerity of the back-bench MPs who stand in their place in the House and foster they myth that the social legislation which is before Parliament and the Canadian public is actually going to help those families who need help the most.
The average family income in 1984 was $35,853. The proposed deindexation will have the effect of saving an estimated $49.5 million in 1986. In other words, that is contrary to what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) promised at the beginning of the debate on universality some 15 months ago. It is also contrary to what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) indicated at that time. More damning is the fact that when the Minister of National Health and Welfare assumed the mantle of his office he did so to represent not only his own constituents but those in our society who need help the most. The Hon. Member opposite from Edmonton laughs. If politicians are to be believed in this world, then they should at least live up the campaign promises that they make. That is why the Canadian public no longer trusts the Government. The Government continually breaks its promises.

speechtext:
The Hon. Member does not want to hear the truth. He raised a technical question with the Hon. Member for Vancouver East and now that he has had the benefit of a technical response he wants to lapse back into some general philosophical discussion.
The point is that the Minister of Health promised the Canadian public 15 months ago that any moneys found-any savings as a result of the review of the child benefits program-would never be used to reduce the size of the federal deficit. Yet, that is exactly what occurred six months later, when, on May 23, the Minister of Finance introduced a
January 20, 1986

Budget which will widen the gap between the rich and the poor in our society. The Minister of Health now has the gall to defend the measures in Bill C-70 while being conspicuously silent on the even more damaging effects Bill C-84 will have on family incomes in the country.
Having said that, I would like to end my remarks on some of the general formalities. At the very beginning of this debate I indicated to Members of the House that the intent of the Government was laudatory. When the child benefits package was referred to committe, members of the committee were asked to consult as widely as possible with various groups across the country and make recommendations to the federal Government suggesting ways and means by which the family allowance, the child tax credit and the child tax exemption could be altered to ensure that more money could be put into the hands of those families who need it the most. That was the original laudatory intent at the beginning of the debate on the child benefits package.
I have indicated to Hon. Members before that when we received that mandate from the federal Government the committee spent, if I am not mistaken, some nine or ten weeks listening to various groups from across the country. The groups and individuals who appeared before the committee did so in the belief that if they gave proper advice, and if we were able to wade through the various testimony, that the three political parties could come up with a better package to recommend to the Minister of Health in order to change the child benefits package. We did so.
With respect to the child tax credit, we recommended that the Government significantly improve the package because we happen to believe it is a socially progressive way by which we can put more money into the hands of poor families. We also recommended that the Government look seriously at eliminating the child tax exemption so that any savings which would result to either the federal Government or the provincial Governments would be funneled into lower income groups. Those were the recommendations of the committee to the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
Frankly, it seems that we wasted our time in that committee because not one of the general directional recommendations which we made was accepted by the Minister, or the committee on planning and priorities when it considered proposals not only to deindex personal exemptions but, worse still, to deindex the family allowances and old age pensions. Largely because of the senior citizens in the country who were so outraged by the thought of having their pensions deindexed, we were able to mount such a successful campaign that the Government had no choice but to back off with its plans. I take it what the Government decided to do was to hang tough, so to speak, with respect to the equally negative effects that this Bill will have on family benefits.
As I mentioned at the beginning of my speech this afternoon, despite the fact that the petition campaign which was launched was the most successful in Canada's history, in which we received between approximately 100,000 and 150,000 signatures, the Government's plan to deindex family allowances
Family Allowances Act, 1973
stands. This Government remains committed to the direction it established fiscally on the night of May 23.
What 1 think is most disturbing about the debate is the following. The blank cheque which Canadians gave to the Conservative Party on September 4, 1984, to institute fundamental change in order that Canadians who are not as well versed in the problems facing social programs in the country said, in essence, to the Conservative Party: "We are giving you authorization for change to these systems".
I had hoped when we began the debate on the review of family and seniors' benefits that all three political parties could have recommended a much better system. I believe we could have recommended a system such as the one referred to by the Hon. Member for Vancouver East. She indicated to the House, and I reiterate, that time and time again professional groups in Canada have come before the Government, not only this one but others, to put forward proposals which would achieve the goals and objectives which were originally established when the debate on child benefits began. That was, namely, to put more into the hands of those who need it the most. It seems to me that if the objective of the exercise is to fundamentally alter the social policy of this country, then the time is right for that kind of debate.
The Budget which was tabled on the night of May 23, 1985, gives us the following lesson. If we are going to create the fundamental will to change the social benefit structures, then fundamental to the success of that objective must be the political support of middle-income Canadians. In order to achieve that political support, the perception and reality must be widely held by middle-income Canadians that the burden of deficit reduction will be shared equally by the corporate sector and by personal income. That, in essence, is where the Conservative Government failed. It failed because it misunderstood the feelings of middle-income Canadians who recognized that in order to deal with the problem of deficit reduction there would have to be some altering of the social programs. What they are asking is if the Government intends middle-income Canadians to expect to have changes in those programs, then the Government must be equally committed to a reform of the Income Tax system so that the corporate sector takes on its fair share of the burden. Until the day occurs on which a Minister of Finance rises in the House of Commons and indicates that the corporate sector of this country will have to assume its fair share of the burden of tax, I feel the Government is going to have a difficult time creating the political will to undertake the necessary reforms to our social benefits structure.
I say that in a particular sense. What I have gathered from my travels across the country is that what so incensed middle-income Canadians is that a Budget which was introduced at a time when we were just beginning an economic renewal and growth, would have deindexed the senior citizens, family allowances and personal tax exemptions while at the same time allowing $500,000 worth of capital gains exemption for

January 20, 1986
Family Allowances Act, 1973
individuals. The Government did not once question the loss of tax revenues as a result of tax decisions made by Revenue Canada. It did not question the amount the corporate sector paid toward tax revenues and so it created a system in which the rich will get richer and the poor will get poorer. 1 can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that is no way to generate the political will to undertake the national debate we so badly need. It is not the fault of the Opposition Party. It is the fault of the governing Party for having failed to properly put into perspective the necessary tools so that that debate could have occurred. I can think of no other shame than the failure of the Conservative Government to bring into the House of Commons a social security package which would benefit those lower income groups and achieve the necessary political will in this country. The Government has now lost the opportunity.

Mr. Speaker, the assumption that the Government's introduction of the six and five program led to a decrease in over-all benefits has to be taken into context. When we introduced the six and five legislation, inflation in this country was running in the double digits. Within 11 months of the introduction of the six and five program, inflation had fallen to below 4 per cent.
